planting.note: Divide and transplant clumps in early spring into moist, well-drained soil; it tolerates drier conditions than its mainland cousin S. angustifolium.

directions: Plant small container divisions in a sunny spot with gritty, well-drained soil, since this grass-like iris relative resents soggy winter conditions more than many of its genus. It sends up slender, flattened, blue-green blades and bears small, six-petaled, violet-blue flowers with a bright yellow throat held just above the foliage from late spring into summer. Shear back spent flower stems to tidy the clump and encourage a repeat flush of bloom. It slowly forms a dense tuft and self-seeds lightly in open, sandy or rocky garden spots, making it a good choice for rock gardens and border edges.

planting.note: Set divisions or transplants into well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost; deadhead to extend the early-summer bloom window.

directions: This classic Robinson-strain pyrethrum cultivar bears single, daisy-form flowers in a soft, clear pale pink with a prominent golden-yellow center, held on wiry stems above finely cut, ferny foliage. Plant in full sun and average, well-drained soil, and divide every two to three years in spring to keep clumps vigorous, since older plants tend to decline and flower less freely. It makes an excellent cut flower and blooms earliest among the painted daisies, typically peaking in late spring to early summer before many other perennials get going. Stake in windy sites, as the flower stems are slender relative to the bloom size.

planting.note: Plant in full sun and well-drained soil in spring; this strong cerise-pink selection pairs well with silver-foliage companions.

directions: 'Brenda' is an older Robinson-strain painted daisy selection prized for its vivid, saturated cerise-pink single blooms, a stronger and brighter shade of pink than most seed-grown pyrethrum. Grow it in full sun with sharply drained soil, since wet winter crowns are its main weak point in colder gardens. Cut spent stems back after the main flush to tidy the ferny foliage mound and occasionally coax a light rebloom later in summer. Lift and divide congested clumps every few years in early spring to maintain vigor and flower count.

planting.note: Transplant divisions into moist, humus-rich soil in spring; this sport of 'Tanna' repeats its parent's compact, dark-stemmed habit but in pink.

directions: A pink-flowered sport of the compact burnet cultivar 'Tanna', this selection carries the same dark, wiry stems and neat, bluish pinnate foliage but produces dangling, bottlebrush-like flower spikes in dusky rose-pink rather than maroon-red from midsummer into fall. Plant in consistently moist but well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light shade, and keep it from drying out during hot spells to prevent early leaf scorch. It stays more compact and floriferous than the larger wild species, making it well suited to perennial borders and pollinator plantings. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain bloom density.

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant after all frost danger has passed; the bright chartreuse foliage colors best in full sun.

directions: This foliage-forward four o'clock selection stands out for its bright, lime-chartreuse leaves, which hold their glowing color all season and make a striking contrast plant even before the fragrant trumpet flowers open. Like other four o'clocks, its magenta-pink to rose blooms unfurl in late afternoon and stay open through the night, closing again by mid-morning, and the plant grows from a fleshy tuberous root that can be lifted and stored over winter in cold climates. Give it full sun for the brightest leaf color, since shade dulls the chartreuse tone toward green. It self-seeds readily and tolerates heat and poor soil well once established.
